serious_errors.materiality: A direct widow grant in the quoted conditional provision concerns Dhuj predeceasing the testator, whereas he actually died later. The report correctly states the condition once, so whether its subsequent widow-beneficiary discussion actually misuses that clause, rather than the whole will and prior interpretation, cannot be confirmed.

serious_errors.materiality: The report raises statutory displacement of the will for the non-taluqdari item despite the pleaded special succession route being confined to the four taluqdari properties. It is phrased as uncertainty, and the underlying Act text is unavailable, so an actual erroneous dispositive application to List B is not established.

important_omissions: The report omits the will’s separate land-revenue allocation: Dhuj and his heirs/successors must bear the villages’ revenue and “the estate will have no concern with it” (S619872d86a62). This is relevant contextual evidence for construing the devised holdings apart from the main estate.

Although the report quotes the predecease condition of will paragraph 4, it does not squarely explain that Dhuj survived the testator (1930 versus 1940) and distinguish that contingent wording from the basis for any widow entitlement after Dhuj’s actual death.

The report does not explicitly disclose that the actual texts of Oudh Estates Act §§13-A, 14 and 22(5) are absent from the allowed LAW sources; that limit is especially material where the conclusion calls the asserted brother preference mandatory.
main_answer_reason: The report substantially and accurately reconstructs the five-property scope, the widow’s and brother’s attributed claims, the key will provisions, lower-court findings and appeal history. It properly withholds a target disposition. Its substantive account is incomplete/overreaching where the appellant’s unverified Oudh Act theory is recast in the conclusion as mandatory statutory preference, and it leaves the predecease clause and List B statutory scope insufficiently separated. Unsupported speculative estate analogies are separately labeled without automatically counting them as confirmed serious errors.
uncertainties: The ultimate appellate reasoning and disposition are withheld; no target outcome has been inferred or graded.
The quoted Oudh Estates Act §§13-A, 14 and 22(5) are pleaded or described in the CASE extracts, but their enacted text and applicability are not in the allowed LAW set.
The status of “Supreme Court” based only on the quoted jurisdiction heading cannot be verified from an express tribunal name in the allowed view.
Whether the report’s “or widow” uncertainty concerns grammar or its application outside the clause’s predecease condition is ambiguous.
The precise independent succession rules for the non-taluqdari List B property are not supplied; the lower-court judgment excerpt does not separately analyze B.
The trust-like, fee-simple, and unspecified statutory-limitation suggestions lack corroborating authority; they are tentative hypotheses and were not treated as settled results.
